title: Israel Faces Political Deadlock as Record Turnout Fails to Produce Clear Winner
snippet: Despite the highest voter turnout in over 25 years, Israel's election ended in a tight stalemate, forcing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu into grueling coalition talks as opposition parties eye a path to unseat him.
content:
JERUSALEM — Israelis woke up to a fraught political reality on Wednesday following an election that drew the highest voter turnout in more than a quarter-century, leaving Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu struggling to hold onto power without a clear path to a parliamentary majority.

With roughly 77% of the votes counted, Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party led the pack with 20.8% of the vote, while his chief challenger, centrist former military chief Gadi Eisenkot and his Yashar party, followed with 16.4%. Though Likud remains the single largest party, exit polls and initial counts show Netanyahu’s far-right governing coalition shrinking, setting off weeks of tense political jockeying.

Arab Parties Surge into Kingmaker Position

Nearly 78% of eligible voters cast ballots—the highest participation rate since 1999. The surge reflected deep voter anxiety over the prolonged war in Gaza, deep social divisions over military draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews, and frustration with Netanyahu’s hard-line allies.

The election featured a historic showing by Arab-led political parties, whose constituents make up about 20% of Israel’s population. Their strong performance has placed them at the center of national debate over whether an opposition coalition could rely on Arab support to oust Netanyahu.

Netanyahu forcefully rejected any collaboration with Arab lawmakers in a speech early Wednesday, branding the idea of partnering with them as anti-Zionist. "We must establish a strong, right-wing, nationalist government," Netanyahu declared to his supporters.

A Fractured Opposition Navigates a Tightrope

In contrast, Eisenkot has signaled an openness to working with Arab parties, provided they meet conditions such as recognizing Israel as a Jewish state and condemning extremist groups like Hamas. However, assembling a viable governing bloc remains a formidable task, as several of Eisenkot's potential coalition partners strongly oppose aligning with Arab factions.

If neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot can secure a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat Knesset, Israel could be headed back to the polls early next year—a scenario reminiscent of the political paralysis that triggered five elections between 2019 and 2022.

The final tally, including hundreds of thousands of absentee ballots from military personnel and diplomats, is expected in the coming days before President Isaac Herzog officially tasks a leader with attempting to form the next government.
